column2: Preparations for the Orange River Proclamation
Officials are arranging the extension of Crown authority south of the Vaal.

The Crown administration inherited a treasury whose obligations exceed its regular receipts. District officers now demand arrears from farmers who question the authority collecting them. A summons served on one farm can become the subject of a meeting across an entire ward, and a sale of property may turn a financial dispute into a test of allegiance. Officials insist that roads, courts and public salaries require revenue. The burghers answer that taxation under a government imposed without their consent deepens every grievance left by the proclamation. We must decide whether to press collection or grant relief while the accounts are reviewed.
Suspend collection and review the accounts.

Petitions circulate through the districts, calling for the return of the Volksraad and the republic's independence. Delegates insist that the acceptance of British officials never amounted to the surrender of the people's right to govern themselves. Each meeting gathers signatures, subscriptions and reports of local grievances. Crown officers fear that the committees are becoming a parallel public authority, while the petitioners still hope to secure a hearing without taking up arms. Allowing their deputation to proceed may expose the depth of opposition, restricting it may convince the districts that peaceful representations have reached their limit.
Permit the deputation to carry its petition.

British authority has been restored at Pretoria. With the commandos dispersed and the Crown administration re-established, ministers turn to the frontier south of the Vaal. They intend to bring the Orange Free State under the same imperial direction. Commissioners will prepare a proclamation and arrange the dispatch of officials to Bloemfontein over the coming two months. The Free State's institutions will remain as a dependent administration, but its foreign policy and sovereign authority will pass under British oversight.

The settlement at Pretoria has secured British control north of the Vaal. Two months later, imperial commissioners arrive at Bloemfontein with orders extending that authority to the Orange Free State. The proclamation restores the Orange River Sovereignty under the Crown, ending the republic's independent diplomacy and placing its administration beneath British supervision. District courts, farms and public accounts remain in local hands, but the Volksraad can no longer speak for a sovereign state. Officials promise security and orderly government, burghers see a second republic losing the independence their fathers obtained. The new administration begins its work amid petitions, distrust and the memory of the war across the river.
Place the Orange River Sovereignty under the Crown.

British commissioners have proclaimed the restoration of the Orange River Sovereignty. The government's public offices remain, but their authority now rests beneath imperial supervision. Britain directs external affairs and requires the administration to observe the terms imposed after the defeat of the Transvaal commandos. The republican colours give way to those of the dependent territory. Families and district councils must reckon with the loss of independent government, while officials attempt to keep the courts, revenue offices and public services functioning through the change.
Maintain the districts under the new administration.
